section_or_table: ## Abstract
printed_context: Can two calibrations of an equation of state that reproduce the measured pressures of aqueous amines loaded with carbon dioxide (CO₂) about equally well predict different liquid phases? An electrolyte perturbed-chain statistical associating fluid theory (ePC-SAFT) model of monoethanolamine (MEA) is calibrated first, and its water, CO₂ and inorganic-ion parameters are held fixed while diethanolamine (DEA), methyldiethanolamine (MDEA) and 2-amino-2-methyl-1-propanol (AMP) are each fitted. Phase-stability searches separate calibrations that the pressure deviations do not. For AMP, two fits deviate by 10.3 and 10.5% from the same fitted total pressures, yet the first gives 73 calculated liquid–liquid splits above 353 K, the highest temperature of the fitted loaded-solution pressures, and the second none. For MDEA, changing one shared MEA interaction lowers the deviation of the fitted total pressures from 20.1 to 11.2% but raises that of the CO₂ partial pressures outside the fit from 20.1 to 33.6%, and its searches confirm two calculated splits at states where none was found with the original value. The MEA and DEA models have no detected instability, and DEA is a negative result: with the adopted DEA pure-component and association parameters, no tested water–DEA interaction represents the binary excess enthalpies and bubble pressures together. The four models and their phase searches are offered as a testbed for calibration practice, in which a fit is judged by the phases it predicts as well as by its deviations, rather than as a basis for absorber design.
